scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Computers make decisions with yes or no answers. Today we meet True and False, and the symbols that produce them.

scenes.onScreen: "Yes or no answers": three numbered lines (1. A boolean is True or False; 2. Compare with == != < > <= >=; 3. One equals sign ties a name; two compare) and an analogy card: a bouncer at a beach club who only answers yes or no: are you eighteen or older?
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A boolean is a value that is either True or False. Python makes one whenever you compare two things. Double equals asks, are these the same? Not equals, less than, greater than, and their or equal versions ask other questions. Think of a bouncer at a beach club. The bouncer only says yes or no. One equals sign ties a name to a value. Two equals signs ask a question.

scenes.narration: [HL 1] Age is seventeen. [HL 2] Greater than or equal to eighteen is a question. The answer is False, and we tie that answer to the name adult. [HL 3] Printing adult shows False. [HL 4] Double equals asks, is age seventeen? That is True. [HL 5] Not equals asks, is age different from seventeen? That is False.

code.source:
age = 17
adult = age >= 18
print(adult)
print(age == 17)
print(age != 17)

scenes.onScreen: Two tags, age and adult, tied to an int and a bool
scenes.animation: Name tags pop in with their arrows to the objects (value and type shown, no addresses); when Python reads a name the arrow glows and the object lights up
scenes.narration: Here is the picture. Age is tied to the int seventeen. Adult is tied to a bool, False. A boolean is an object like any number or string. Its type is bool, and it has only two possible values, True and False. Write them with a capital first letter.

scenes.onScreen: beaches.py: comparing strings, and a chained comparison
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] A name tied to Palolem. [HL 2] The same text on both sides, so True. [HL 3] A small letter p is a different character. So this comparison is False. Python is case sensitive for text too. [HL 4] Python even lets you chain. Five is less than ten, and ten is less than twenty. Both are true, so the answer is True.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the command types with key-tick, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as beaches dot py. In the terminal, type python, space, beaches dot py. True, then False, then True.

scenes.narration: Let us recap. One: A boolean is True or False, with a capital first letter. Two: Comparison operators give back booleans. Three: One equals sign ties a name. Two equals signs compare. Four: Text comparisons are case sensitive. Pause the video, and say these ideas out loud, once, slowly.

shorts.title: True or False
shorts.hook: "A boolean is a value that is either True or False."
shorts.script: A boolean is a value that is either True or False. Python gives you one every time you compare two things. Is seventeen bigger than eighteen? False. Is seventeen equal to seventeen? True. The first letter is always a capital. A boolean is a value like any other. You can save it in a name and print it. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Booleans in 40 seconds.

shorts.title: Six comparison symbols
shorts.script: Six symbols make comparisons. Double equals asks, are they the same. Not equals asks, are they different. Less than and greater than compare size. Less than or equal, and greater than or equal, include the same number too. Each one gives back True or False. Learn these six, and you are ready for decisions with if and else. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Six ways to ask.

shorts.title: One equals or two
shorts.hook: "One equals sign and two equals signs are very different."
shorts.script: One equals sign and two equals signs are very different. One equals sign ties a name to a value. It is an instruction. Two equals signs ask a question, are these the same, and give True or False. Say it in your head, equals means tie, double equals means ask. This tiny difference is behind many beginner bugs, so learn it now. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Tie or ask?

shorts.title: Invalid syntax
shorts.script: Here is the bug. You write if age equals eighteen with one equals sign. Python says syntax error, invalid syntax. It even adds a hint, maybe you meant double equals. The if line needs a question, and one equals sign is an instruction, not a question. Use two equals signs, and the program runs. Read the hint, it is very friendly. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Python gives a hint.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the boolean break up with the string?"
shorts.script: Why did the boolean break up with the string? It only wanted a True relationship. Your challenge. Make score equal fifty five. Print whether score is at least forty, and print whether score equals fifty five. You should see two words, in capital letters. Try changing score to thirty, and run again. Post your code in the comments. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 11.
